questions.q: What did one have to do if he sinned against his neighbor?
questions.a: If a person sinned against his neighbor, on the day that he recognizes his guilt, he must restore whatever he took or the lost thing that he had found and add a fifth more value to what he restores or returns.

questions.q: What must one do who swore falsely about any matter?
questions.a: If one swore concerning something as a lie, he must restore the full value and add one-fifth of its value to it.

questions.q: What should someone bring to the priest for a guilt offering if he is guilty of the sins above?
questions.a: If one is guilty of the sins above, he must bring a purifying offering, a perfect ram from the flock.

questions.q: How long must the burnt offering remain on the altar?
questions.a: The burnt offering must remain burning on the altar all night, until the morning.

questions.q: What must the priest wear to remove the fatty ash from the altar?
questions.a: The priest must put on his linen robe and underclothes to remove the ashes from the altar.

questions.q: What must the priest do before carrying the ashes outside the camp?
questions.a: The priest had to take off his linen clothes and put on other clothes before taking the fatty ash outside of the camp.

questions.q: What must be kept going at all times?
questions.a: The fire on the altar must be made to burn on the alter; it must not go out.

questions.q: What should the priests to do with the leftover unleavened bread?
questions.a: In a holy place; in the courtyard of the tent of meeting, Aaron and his sons should eat the unleavened bread.

questions.q: What do the sons of Aaron have to do when their sons are anointed?
questions.a: The sons of Aaron must present a grain offering of a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour, half in the morning and half in the evening.

questions.q: How must this grain offering be prepared?
questions.a: This grain offering must be combined with oil and made on a griddle in oil.

questions.q: Who would offer this grain offering?
questions.a: The priest who is in line to succeed the current high priest should perform the grain offering in this way.

questions.q: According to the law of the sin offering, what did the priest have to do to the offering?
questions.a: The priest had to eat the sin offering in the courtyard of the tent of meeting.

questions.q: What had to be done with the clay pot in which the meat was boiled?
questions.a: The clay pot in which the meat was boiled had to be shattered.

questions.q: What part of the sin offering was not to be eaten?
questions.a: No part of the sin offering was to be eaten from which blood was brought into the tent of meeting to make atonement in the holy place.

commentary.text: Verses 1–7 Though all the instances relate to our neighbour, yet it is called a trespass against the Lord. Though the person injured be mean, and even despicable, yet the injury reflects upon that God who has made the command of loving our neighbour next to that of loving himself. Human laws make a difference as to punishments; but all methods of doing wrong to others, are alike violations of the Divine law, even keeping what is found, when the owner can be discovered. Frauds are generally accompanied with lies, often with false oaths. If the offender would escape the vengeance of God, he must make ample restitution, according to his power, and seek forgiveness by faith in that one Offering which taketh away the sin of the world. The trespasses here mentioned, still are trespasses against the law of Christ, which insists as much upon justice and truth, as the law of nature, or the law of Moses.

The daily sacrifice of a lamb is chiefly referred to. The priest must take care of the fire upon the altar. The first fire upon the altar came from heaven, ch. 9:24; by keeping that up continually, all their sacrifices might be said to be consumed with the fire from heaven, in token of God's acceptance. Thus should the fire of our holy affections, the exercise of our faith and love, of prayer and praise, be without ceasing.

The law of the burnt-offerings put upon the priests a great deal of care and work; the flesh was wholly burnt, and the priests had nothing but the skin. But most of the meat-offering was their own. It is God's will that his ministers should be provided with what is needful.

The blood of the sin-offering was to be washed out of the clothes on which it should happen to be sprinkled, which signified the regard we ought to have to the blood of Christ, not counting it a common thing. The vessel in which the flesh of the sin-offering was boiled must be broken, if it were an earthen one; but if a brazen one, well washed. This showed that the defilement was not wholly taken away by the offering; but the blood of Christ thoroughly cleanses from all sin. All these rules set forth the polluting nature of sin, and the removal of guilt from the sinner to the sacrifice. Behold and wonder at Christ's love, in that he was content to be made a sin-offering for us, and so to procure our pardon for continual sins and failings. He that knew no sin was made sin (that is, a sin-offering) for us, 2Co 5:21. Hence we have pardon, and not only pardon, but power also, against sin, Ro 8:3.
